blocks.prompt: The Egg in the Pouch
blocks.text: Almost every animal with fur has live babies. The echidna does not. The echidna lays one egg. The egg is soft, not hard, and about the size of a grape. She rolls the egg into a little pouch on her belly. Ten days later the egg hatches. The baby is called a puggle. It has no spines yet. It is pink and smaller than a jelly bean. The puggle drinks milk in the pouch. The milk comes right out of its mom's skin, because an echidna has no nipples. In about seven weeks the puggle grows spines. Then its mom digs a warm burrow and tucks it inside.

blocks.prompt: The Animal With No Teeth
blocks.text: An echidna has no teeth. Not one. Its whole face narrows into a hard beak about as long as your thumb, and inside that beak is a tongue longer than your hand. The tongue is coated in sticky spit. When an echidna finds a termite nest, it rips the wall open with its claws and flicks its tongue in and out, faster than you can count. Ants and termites stick to it and get pulled back in. The echidna grinds them between hard pads at the back of its tongue and the roof of its mouth. That is how it chews without teeth. Finding the nest is the clever part. Every living thing gives off tiny electric signals when its muscles move. The tip of an echidna's beak is packed with sensors that pick up those signals through wet soil. The echidna does not need to see its dinner. It can feel the bugs moving underground. If something big comes along, the echidna does not run. It is slow. Instead it digs straight down, all four feet working at once, and sinks into the dirt like a stone into mud. In under a minute, only a pad of spines is left showing at the surface.

blocks.prompt: The Animal Nobody Believed
blocks.text: There are more than six thousand kinds of mammal alive today. All of them have hair. All of them make milk. And all but five give birth to live young. Those five are the monotremes: the platypus, and the four kinds of echidna. They are mammals that lay eggs. For a long time, Europeans refused to believe it. When the first echidna specimens reached London in the 1790s, the reports sounded like a joke: a furry animal with a beak and spines that hatched out of an egg. Scientists named it after Echidna, a monster in Greek myth who was half woman and half snake, because the creature seemed to be half one thing and half another. It took nearly a century of arguing before Europeans accepted that the egg was real. Aboriginal Australians had known it all along. The truth is stranger than the joke. Echidnas are not failed mammals or leftover reptiles. Their branch split away from the rest of the mammal family roughly one hundred and eighty million years ago, long before Tyrannosaurus or Triceratops existed, and it has been running ever since. The egg is not a mistake nobody got around to fixing. It is simply how this branch has always done it, and it has worked for a very long time. An echidna's body also runs cool, around eighty-nine degrees Fahrenheit, the lowest of any mammal. In cold weather it can drop even lower and shut itself down for weeks, breathing slowly, waiting. Echidnas have survived bushfires this way, sunk into a burrow while the fire passed over the top of them.

blocks.prompt: How to Raise a Puggle
blocks.text: Echidna mating season starts in the middle of the Australian winter, and it looks like a parade. A female moves through the bush and a line of males forms behind her, nose to tail, sometimes as many as ten, following her for days and even weeks. Naturalists call it an echidna train. She may drag the train around for a month before she chooses. About three weeks later she lays a single egg. She does not build a nest for it. She curls her body and rolls the egg straight from her belly into a shallow pouch, a fold of skin that only appears when she needs it and flattens away again when she is done. The egg is leathery rather than brittle, and roughly the size of a grape. Ten days later the egg splits. What comes out is barely an animal: a pink, blind, jelly-bean-sized creature called a puggle, with no spines and no fur, gripping its mother's skin with front feet that are already surprisingly strong. There is nothing for it to nurse from. Echidnas have no nipples. Instead, milk seeps out through patches of skin, and the puggle laps it up from her fur. Echidna milk is pink, tinted by iron. The puggle rides in the pouch for about seven weeks, drinking and growing fast. Then its spines begin to push through, and its mother evicts it, for fairly obvious reasons. She digs a nursery burrow, tucks the puggle inside, plugs the entrance with soil, and leaves. She returns roughly every five days to feed it, then seals it up and goes again. This continues for about seven months. Then the young echidna walks out of the burrow and is on its own. It is a slow, expensive way to produce one animal. But echidnas can live past forty years, which is extraordinary for something the size of a football, so they can afford to take their time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

Electroreceptors in the beak detect prey through wet soil
Cloaca: one opening for waste and eggs

blocks.prompt: The Case Against Calling the Echidna Primitive
blocks.text: For most of the last two hundred years, the echidna has been described as primitive. The word turns up constantly in older textbooks: a primitive mammal, a living fossil, a halfway creature stalled somewhere between reptile and mammal. It is an easy story to tell. The echidna lays an egg, as a reptile does. It has a single opening, the cloaca, for waste and for eggs, as a reptile does. Its legs stick out sideways from its body rather than underneath it, and it walks with the rolling gait of an animal that seems not quite finished. Its body runs cool, around eighty-nine degrees Fahrenheit, the lowest of any mammal. Put those facts in a row and the conclusion looks obvious. The conclusion is wrong, and the reason it is wrong is worth understanding, because the same mistake gets made about a lot of animals. Start with time. The monotremes, meaning the platypus and the four species of echidna, split from the rest of the mammal family roughly one hundred and eighty million years ago. That is not a small detail. It means the echidna is not our ancestor and never was. It is our very distant cousin, and it has had exactly as long to evolve as we have. Every day our branch spent inventing placentas and nipples and hot, fast bodies, the echidna's branch spent doing something else. Not less. Different. Look at what it did with the time. An echidna's beak is studded with electroreceptors, sensors that detect the faint electrical crackle a termite's muscles make when they move. No dog has this. No human has this. The echidna can locate food it cannot see, smell, or hear, through solid wet ground. Its tongue, which shoots out several inches and retracts dozens of times a minute, is coated in sticky mucus and grinds prey against hard pads, because teeth were not worth keeping. It has a claw on each hind foot lengthened specifically for reaching between its own spines to groom. None of that is leftover. All of it is engineering. The cool body is the same story. Running at eighty-nine degrees costs less fuel than running at ninety-eight. An echidna eats ants and termites, which are small and not especially nourishing, so a cheap body is a sensible body. When conditions turn hard, it can drop its temperature further and enter torpor, shutting down for weeks at a time. Echidnas have been recorded surviving bushfires this way, sunk in a burrow while the fire passed overhead. Try that with a mouse. Even the egg is not a relic nobody bothered to fix. It is a strategy. A leathery egg, incubated in a pouch that grows only when it is needed, hatching a puggle the size of a jelly bean, is a low-cost and low-risk way to start a life, and echidnas live long enough, sometimes past forty years, to do it slowly and repeatedly. The honest summary is this. The echidna is not an early draft of a mammal. It is a finished animal from a different lineage, solving a life we do not live, using tools we do not have. Calling it primitive says more about the ranking than it says about the echidna. And the ranking has consequences. The four species are not equally safe. The short-beaked echidna is common across Australia, but the long-beaked echidnas of New Guinea are in serious trouble, and one of them, Attenborough's long-beaked echidna, went unseen by scientists for more than sixty years. A camera trap finally photographed it in the Cyclops Mountains in 2023, alive the whole time, in a forest nobody had checked.
